argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0109d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0109.

PROJECT
The team is designing a bike-share docking station app.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Industrial Designer (ID)  Tomas  present
B  User Interface designer (UI)  Priya  present
C  Marketing Expert (ME)  Hannah  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Marcus  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0109a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting and the team introduced themselves. He presented the project: a rider-facing app for a city bike-share scheme's docking stations. The pilot covers fourteen docking stations in the city centre. The app has three core functions: find a bike, unlock it at the dock, and return it and pay. It must run on both iOS and Android. After a short whiteboard exercise, the team discussed first ideas. These covered how the phone connects to the dock (QR code, Bluetooth or NFC), use outdoors in all weather and at night, one-tap unlocking, and moving payment setup to sign-up. A leaderboard idea from the industrial designer was parked as out of scope for the pilot. The next meeting was first set for Wednesday at nine. It was later moved to Friday at ten so that the marketing expert's rider survey results would be available.
  decisions: The next meeting (functional design) will be on Friday at ten. This replaces the earlier plan of Wednesday at nine. Payment setup will happen at sign-up, so that at the dock the rider only needs to unlock. Unlocking should be possible in about one tap after opening the app.
  actions: The industrial designer will ask the dock supplier how the phone connects to the dock and whether the dock has a screen. The user interface designer will produce rough wireframes of the main flows: find, unlock and return. The marketing expert will send a quick survey to the pilot waiting list, including one question on the leaderboard idea. The marketing expert will review competitor bike-share apps and their user reviews. The project manager will send out the minutes, the project brief and the shared folder link.
  problems: The dock hardware is still unknown, including the connection method (QR, Bluetooth or NFC) and whether the dock has a screen. This must be confirmed with the supplier. QR-based unlocking may fail in rain, and the screens must be readable outdoors and at night. It is unclear whether riders want a leaderboard feature. It was parked pending survey feedback.
  action item SY0109a.ai1: Contact the dock supplier to find out how the phone connects to the dock (QR, Bluetooth, NFC) and whether the dock has a screen (owner A, active)
  action item SY0109a.ai2: Sketch rough wireframes of the main user flows: find, unlock, return (owner B, active)
  action item SY0109a.ai3: Send a quick rider survey to the pilot waiting list, including one question on the leaderboard idea (owner C, active)
  action item SY0109a.ai4: Review competitor bike-share apps and their user reviews (owner C, active)
  action item SY0109a.ai5: Send out the meeting minutes, the project brief and the shared folder link (owner D, active)
  fact (plan_change): The next meeting was first agreed for Wednesday at nine. It was moved to Friday at ten because the survey results would not be back until Thursday.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed a leaderboard of kilometres ridden. The project manager parked it as out of scope for the pilot.

[SY0109b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting and confirmed he had sent out the kickoff minutes, the brief and the shared folder link. The industrial designer reported back from the dock supplier: the docks use Bluetooth Low Energy with a QR sticker as backup, there is no NFC, and there is no screen, only an LED ring. The team chose Bluetooth as the main unlock method with QR as the fallback. The user interface designer presented rough wireframes for the find, unlock and return flows. The marketing expert presented the rider survey results: the top request was seeing free return slots, the second was knowing the price before a ride, and only about eighteen percent were interested in a leaderboard. The leaderboard was dropped for the pilot. The marketing expert's competitor review showed that most one-star reviews concern failed unlocks and returns that were never registered. This led the team to add a proper return confirmation screen showing the cost. The project manager summarised the functions: find with bikes and free slots on the map, one-tap Bluetooth unlock with QR fallback and the price shown beforehand, and return with confirmation. Payment stays at sign-up, and a high-contrast mode will be added for night use. The next meeting was set for Tuesday at two.
  decisions: Bluetooth will be the main way to unlock a bike, with the dock's QR sticker as the fallback. The leaderboard is dropped for the pilot, given weak survey interest. The map will show free return slots as well as available bikes. The return flow will end with a confirmation screen stating that the bike is locked, the ride has ended and what was paid. The price will be shown to the rider before unlocking. Payment setup stays at sign-up, as agreed at the kickoff. The app will have a high-contrast mode for night use. If Bluetooth is off on the phone, the app will prompt the rider to switch it on. The next meeting (conceptual design) will be on Tuesday at two.
  actions: The industrial designer will ask the dock supplier how long it takes for a dock to report a return. The user interface designer will update the wireframes. The updates are: free slots on the map, a return confirmation with the cost, the price before unlock, a QR fallback screen, and a prompt to switch on Bluetooth. The user interface designer will check guidance on outdoor readability, such as contrast and text size. This task was first given to the marketing expert. The marketing expert will upload the survey results and the competitor review notes to the shared folder. The project manager will send out the minutes and an invite for the next meeting.
  problems: It is not yet known how quickly a dock reports a return to the system. This matters for the return confirmation. The Bluetooth range is only about two metres, so riders must stand at the dock. Riders may not understand the dock's LED colours, so the phone has to carry all feedback. The QR fallback remains unreliable in rain and at night. The readability standards for outdoor and night use still need to be checked.
  action item SY0109b.ai1: Ask the dock supplier how long it takes for a dock to report a returned bike to the system (owner A, active)
  action item SY0109b.ai2: Update the wireframes: free slots on the map, a return confirmation with the cost, the price before unlock, a QR fallback screen and a Bluetooth-on prompt (owner B, active)
  action item SY0109b.ai3: Check guidance on outdoor readability (contrast, text size) for the high-contrast mode (owner B, reassigned)
  action item SY0109b.ai4: Upload the survey results and the competitor review notes to the shared folder (owner C, active)
  action item SY0109b.ai5: Send out the minutes and an invite for the next meeting (owner D, active)

[SY0109c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting and explained that the user interface designer was absent all week on an accessibility training course. He confirmed that the minutes and invite had been sent, and the marketing expert confirmed that the survey results and competitor notes were in the shared folder. The industrial designer reported that a dock normally reports a return within ten seconds, but this can take up to about two minutes when mobile signal is poor, notably at the two docks in the underground station car park. To handle this, the team designed a two-stage return confirmation: the phone shows 'bike locked' at once via the dock's Bluetooth lock status, the cost follows when the system confirms, a receipt notification is sent if confirmation is slow, and billing stops at the lock time. On look and feel, the team chose the council's teal as the brand colour, with green and red reserved for status, and a night mode that follows the phone's dark mode setting with an in-app toggle. The marketing expert took over the outdoor readability check from the absent user interface designer, and the next meeting was set for Monday at eleven.
  decisions: The return confirmation has two stages: 'bike locked' is shown immediately based on the dock's Bluetooth lock status, and the cost is shown once the system confirms the return. If the system has not confirmed after about thirty seconds, the app tells the rider a receipt will follow and sends a notification when it arrives. Rides are billed up to the moment the bike locks, not when the dock's message reaches the system. Teal from the council's brand guidelines is the app's brand colour for buttons and headers, and green and red are used only for status. The exact shades are pending the user interface designer's review. The high-contrast night mode follows the phone's own dark mode setting, with a manual toggle in the app. No sponsor logo will appear on the confirmation screen for the pilot. The outdoor readability check is reassigned from the user interface designer to the marketing expert. The next meeting (detailed design) will be on Monday at eleven. This replaces the project manager's initial suggestion of Friday at two.
  actions: The industrial designer will confirm with the dock supplier that the dock sends its lock status to the phone over Bluetooth. The industrial designer will ask the supplier whether the mobile signal at the underground car park docks can be boosted. The user interface designer (absent) will add the 'bike locked, confirming' state and the receipt notification to the wireframes. The marketing expert will do the outdoor readability check (contrast, text size), taking it over from the user interface designer. The marketing expert will chase the council for the final brand guidelines (colours and logo). The project manager will send out the minutes, brief the user interface designer on the decisions and ask for her view on the teal shades. The project manager will send an invite for the next meeting on Monday at eleven.
  problems: It is not yet confirmed that the dock sends its lock status to the phone over Bluetooth. The two-stage return confirmation depends on this. The mobile signal at the two underground car park docks is poor, so returns there may take up to about two minutes to register. The accent colour for the night mode main button (yellow or bright teal on black) is unresolved until the readability check is done. The council's brand guidelines are only a draft, and the exact teal shades still need the user interface designer's contrast review.
  action item SY0109c.ai1: Confirm with the dock supplier that the dock sends its lock status (with lock timestamp) to the phone over Bluetooth (owner A, active)
  action item SY0109c.ai2: Ask the dock supplier whether the mobile signal at the underground car park docks can be boosted (owner A, active)
  action item SY0109c.ai3: Add the 'bike locked, confirming' pending state and the receipt notification to the wireframes (owner B, active)
  action item SY0109c.ai4: Check guidance on outdoor readability (contrast, text size) for the colour scheme and high-contrast mode (owner C, reassigned)
  action item SY0109c.ai5: Chase the council for the final brand guidelines (colours and logo) (owner C, active)
  action item SY0109c.ai6: Send out the minutes, brief the absent user interface designer on the decisions and ask for her view on the teal shades (owner D, active)
  action item SY0109c.ai7: Send an invite for the next meeting (detailed design) on Monday at eleven (owner D, active)
  fact (absence): The user interface designer (Priya) was absent all week because she was on an accessibility training course.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer proposed using the phone's light sensor to switch to high-contrast mode automatically. The project manager found it too fiddly, and the team followed the phone's own setting instead.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a sponsor logo on the confirmation screen. It was parked as not for the pilot.
  fact (plan_change): The project manager first suggested Friday at two for the next meeting. It was moved to Monday at eleven because the user interface designer's course runs until Friday.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_SELF_CORRECTION [F1]: A speaker states a fact or number, then corrects themselves ("sorry, I mean ...") within the same or the next turn. The gold summary must use the corrected value.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_PLAN_CHANGE [F1]: The team agrees on a plan early in the meeting, then later in the same meeting changes it (different choice, date, or approach). The gold summary must state only the FINAL plan, and may mention that it was revised.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.


A PREVIOUS ATTEMPT AT THIS MEETING FAILED VALIDATION (attempt 2 of 3). Write the whole meeting again from scratch, and fix these problems:
- F1_SELF_CORRECTION: self-correction segments must share one speaker, got ['A', 'D']
